title.narrative: Haiti - ACJR 2024 (Project)

description.narrative: In Turgeau (PaP), the focus will be on enhancing the protective environment despite the continued threats to life, aiming to complement IRC/SV’s work on WASH, Health and SGBV prevention / response, while providing short-term relief through MPC. In Jacmel, LAPDEFF and Plan will also provide direct Case Management to support the government institution IBERS’ limited capacity there, and will work with IBERS to set up a Child Protection Working Group in Jacmel.

Protection activities include psychological first aid (PFA) and recreational activities (through Child-Friendly Spaces, CFS), as well as case management (CM) and family tracing and reunification (FTR) in collaboration with IBESR (a government institution), but also provision of dignity kits and prevention activities, primarily through community-based mechanisms. The same activities will be implemented in Jacmel, but with a greater focus on community integration, as well as regaining a level of stability without familiar support networks, and building instead on Plan and LAPDEFF’s own ongoing interventions and pre-existing structures.
The project focuses on reuniting unaccompanied and/or separated children with their caregivers or placing them in appropriate protective care settings. Furthermore, it aims to offer customized support to children tailored to their individual needs. 300 UASCs, children survivors of SGBV and other forms of violence and abuse, are identified, registered, assessed, and referred (PaP) or provided with direct case management services (Jacmel). Children will be provided with services such as psychosocial support or referred for health or legal support or MPC support. Case workers, 5 CPCs and IBESR will be capacitated to support this process. Based on needs, 100 children will be provided with dignity kits. In addition, family tracing and reunification process will be initiated for 80 Unaccompanied Asylum Seeking Children. 8 accredited temporary foster families will be supported to provide quality alternative care. Post-reunification follow-up visits will be conducted for reunified children.
Besides, 1 mobile Child-Friendly Space (CFS) and 4 fixed CFS will be established and managed in PaP and Jacmel to provide PSS, including PFA, and group activities for child well-being to 3000 crisis-affected and displaced children by 25 trained CFS facilitators, under supervision of the CPIE officers. CFS will also be used to provide information on how to prevent identified CP risks, especially separation and gender-based violence and disseminate available referral pathways as well as to identify and refer children with protection concerns.
Additionally, the initiative aims to improve the socio-economic well-being and resilience of a substantial number of beneficiaries through unconditional and unrestricted cash transfers. Multipurpose cash will target 450 of the most vulnerable households identified through the protection activities, using a 1-time payment of 75% of the MEB (270 USD), aligned with WV’s ACJR intervention and coordinated with the Cash Working Group as well as TF, who will use a different approach to cover different needs. The activity includes sensitization and conflict-sensitivity measures and will target 80% IDPs. It will be coupled with the standard elements described in the narrative, including the complaint and feedback mechanism, a direct monitoring survey to ensure the distribution is received well, and a Post Distribution Monitoring 1 to maximum 3 weeks later. In line with the needs, 350 HHs in Turgeau will receive MPC from CAPAC while 100 HHs in Jacmel will receive MPC from Plan

SUMMARY In response to escalating insecurity, internal displacement, food shortages, and the breakdown of essential services, the Dutch Relief Alliance initiated a Joint Response, in which Plan International is participating. Plan International’s activities in Haiti are focused on protection and Multipurpose Cash (MPC) Assistance and will be implemented in the municipality of Jacmel in the Sud-Est department, and the Turgeau section of the Metropolitan Area of Port-au-Prince in the Ouest department. The project prioritises crisis-related psychosocial support and the identification and referral of children with protection concerns to appropriates services. The project runs from 29 April 2024 to 28 October 2024.

The activities focus on Unaccompanied Asylum Seeking Children, and children survivors of violence and abuse. Children will be provided with services such as psychosocial support, or referred for health or legal support, along with dignity kits based on needs, Multipurpose cash activity targets 450 vulnerable households, with 80% being IDP and 20% host community members.

The humanitarian crisis in Haiti results from escalating insecurity, internal displacement, food shortages, and the breakdown of essential services. In Port-au-Prince, violence perpetrated by armed gangs, compounded by poverty and climate change, has led to a significant increase in internal displacement. The situation further deteriorated with additional displacement during violent attacks in February '24, leaving many residing in overcrowded camps in Port-au-Prince, where dire living conditions exacerbate the spread of diseases. The country has witnessed a staggering increase in internal displacement, with over 362,000 individuals forced to flee their homes due to the violence. Women, girls, and persons with disabilities are disproportionately affected by the crisis, facing heightened risks of exploitation, abuse, and violence. Furthermore, schools, which often serve as safe havens for children, are increasingly targeted for recruitment by gangs, exacerbating the risks faced by vulnerable youth. The situation poses a grave threat to children's safety and well-being, necessitating urgent intervention to ensure their protection. In Jacmel, the situation has generally been more stable, but that has led to a rapid surge in IDPs.

The project supports unaccompanied and/or separated children to be reunited with their caregivers or in appropriate protective care arrangements. Family tracing and reunification process are initiated in collaboration with the local actors. Accredited temporary foster families will be supported to provide quality alternative care. In addition, Child-Friendly Spaces (CFS) are established and managed to provide psychosocial support for well-being of crisis-affected and displaced children by trained CFS facilitators. CFS will also be used to provide information on how to prevent identified protection risks and to disseminate referral pathways. Also, Unaccompanied Asylum Seeking Children, children survivors of violence and abuse, are identified, registered, assessed, and referred (in PaP) or provided with direct case management services (in Jacmel). Based on needs, children are also provided with dignity kits. Besides, multipurpose cash is provided to 450 of the most vulnerable households identified through the protection activities, using a 1-time payment of 270 USD to support with basic needs.

comment.narrative: In this report, more people were reached due to the targeted focus on two highly populated IDP camps—Lycée Marie Jeanne and Lycée des Jeunes Filles—located within densely affected areas of Port-au-Prince. The collaboration between CAPAC and Plan International enabled comprehensive mobilization efforts, ensuring broad participation across age groups through organized focus groups and interviews. Additionally, the streamlined methodology, combining direct observation with key informant interviews, allowed for a thorough assessment that captured the needs of a larger cross-section of the population within these sites.

Tailor Child-Friendly Space (CFS) activities to include targeted programs specifically designed for children and adolescents. Increase the cash assistance amount to approximatelu 35,000 goudes to provide more substantial support.

comment.narrative:
The diverse range of activities offered through this program fostered extensive engagement and high levels of participation across all age groups. By providing creative, educational, and social development opportunities tailored to different age categories, from young children to adolescents, we created an inclusive environment that attracted substantial community involvement. Additionally, awareness-raising sessions for parents and displaced individuals, along with targeted support for vulnerable groups, such as teenage mothers and at-risk youth, reinforced the program’s reach and accessibility.
This comprehensive approach resonated strongly within the community, encouraging families and individuals to actively participate and maximize the resources available to them. As a result, participation exceeded initial expectations, allowing us to achieve over 100% of our target reach. The combination of structured activities, parental engagement, and culturally relevant content made the program highly effective in meeting—and surpassing—its intended goals.

comment.narrative: The project was implemented across two IDP sites, which occasionally faced security issues, particularly at Lycée des Jeunes. Consequently, the partner organization frequently had to suspend team deployments until the security situation was stabilized. This limited the team’s ability to reach targeted children for case management as planned.

title.narrative: Support to separated/unaccompanied children
Number of unaccompanied and/or separated children who are reunited with their caregivers OR in appropriate protective care arrangements based on BIA

comment.narrative: At the start of the project, IBESR determined that each identified Unaccompanied and Separated Child (UASC) should only be reunified once the reunification environment was confirmed safe, to prevent any risk of further harm. Identified children were placed in alternative care with foster families within the IDP sites. However, by project’s end, only 8 children (5 girls and 3 boys) were reunified by IBESR, supported by the project’s financial and material resources.
